title: Building an AI Research Tool — The Full Lifecycle

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

This lesson walks you through the complete lifecycle of building a real, working AI-powered research tool — from a vague idea to a deployed system. You'll learn how to:

- Use AI to plan, scope, and write requirements for a technical tool
- Have AI generate a full system architecture (C4 model diagrams, architecture decision records)
- Run exhaustive iterative review cycles across security, scalability, reliability, and UX
- Force AI to review in genuine depth — not just surface validation
- Generate a detailed implementation plan with dependencies and risk buffers
- Review and stress-test the implementation plan before a single line of code is written
- Build the tool itself using AI as your implementation partner throughout
- Have AI review every piece of code before it is accepted — systematically, not superficially
- Verify the tool actually builds and runs before declaring it done

This is the methodology professional AI engineers use when building production systems with AI assistance. You'll apply it to a concrete research tool: an AI research assistant that decomposes questions, searches multiple sources in parallel, triangulates claims across sources, and produces a cited report.

## The Tool We're Building

The target: a **multi-source AI research assistant** that takes a research question and returns a cited report in under 60 seconds.

Capabilities:
- Decomposes a complex question into 3–5 specific sub-questions
- Searches Perplexity, Exa AI, and Tavily in parallel (one per sub-question)
- Merges findings and detects contradictions between sources
- Produces a report with every claim linked to a source URL

This tool is genuinely useful and non-trivial to build correctly. It involves parallel API calls, multi-agent coordination, and claim verification — making it an ideal vehicle for the full architecture-to-implementation lifecycle.

**Who this applies to beyond this tool:**
The methodology you'll learn — plan → AI-architect → deep review → implement plan → build — applies to any substantial AI project: a document analysis pipeline, a customer support agent, an automated workflow, a personal data assistant. The tool is the vehicle; the process is the lesson.

## Phase 1: Requirements — Using AI to Scope What You're Building

Before writing any architecture, you need clear requirements. Vague requirements produce vague architectures. AI can help you surface the requirements you haven't thought of yet.

**Step 1 — Write the initial brief:**
```
I want to build an AI research tool. Here's my rough idea:
[describe your tool in 3–5 sentences]

Help me turn this into structured requirements by asking me clarifying questions.
Focus on: who uses it, how they trigger it, what inputs they provide,
what outputs they expect, and what happens when things go wrong.
```

**Step 2 — Extract functional requirements:**
```
Based on our discussion, write the functional requirements for this tool.
Format:
- FR-01: [User can do X]
- FR-02: [System must do Y]
- FR-03: [Tool returns Z]
...

For each, add: Priority (Must Have / Should Have / Nice to Have)
```

**Step 3 — Surface the hidden non-functional requirements:**
Non-functional requirements (NFRs) are often invisible in the brief but dominate the architecture.

```
For this tool description: [paste brief]

Identify the non-functional requirements that aren't stated but are implied.
For each, specify:
- What the requirement is
- Why it's implied (not stated but needed)
- What the most likely acceptable threshold is
- What breaks if we ignore it

Focus on: latency, accuracy, cost per query, reliability, concurrency, data privacy.
```

**What AI typically surfaces for a research tool:**

| NFR | Likely threshold | What breaks if ignored |
|-----|-----------------|------------------------|
| Response latency | < 60 seconds (async acceptable) | Users think it's broken or give up |
| Citation accuracy | < 5% hallucinated URLs | Core credibility is destroyed |
| Cost per query | < $0.10 | Unsustainable at any real scale |
| Concurrency | 10–50 simultaneous users | System collapses under light load |
| API rate limit handling | Graceful degradation | Crashes when one provider throttles |

## Phase 2: AI-Assisted Architecture Design

With requirements in hand, have AI generate the system architecture. The key insight: scope each prompt to one abstraction level. Mixing levels produces confused, unusable diagrams.

**Prompt 1 — System Context (Level 1):**
```
Design the system context for this AI research tool:
[paste requirements]

Output a Mermaid C4Context diagram showing:
- The primary user persona
- The research tool system
- External systems it depends on (search APIs, LLMs, etc.)
- Data flows between them

Keep this level abstract — system-to-system interactions only, no internals.
```

**Prompt 2 — Container Architecture (Level 2):**
```
Now design the container architecture for the research tool internals.
Keep the same Mermaid C4 format.

Containers to include:
- API Gateway (entry point)
- Research Orchestrator (manages the research pipeline)
- Question Decomposer (breaks question into sub-questions)
- Parallel Search Agents (one per sub-question)
- Claims Verifier (triangulates sources)
- Report Generator (produces final output)
- Result Cache (optional, for repeated queries)

For each container, show: technology stack, responsibility, and connections.
```

**Prompt 3 — Architecture Decision Records:**
For every major design choice, generate an ADR (Architecture Decision Record). ADRs document WHY you made each decision — they're invaluable when the team asks "why did we build it this way?" six months later.

```
For this architecture, identify the 5 most important decisions that need to be documented.
For each, write an ADR in this format:

## ADR-001: [Decision Title]
**Status:** Proposed
**Context:** [Why this decision was needed]
**Decision:** [What we decided]
**Alternatives considered:** [Other options evaluated]
**Rationale:** [Why this option over the others]
**Consequences:** [What this enables, what it rules out, what risks remain]
```

**Example ADRs for a research tool:**
- ADR-001: Parallel vs. sequential search execution
- ADR-002: Which search APIs to integrate (Perplexity vs. Exa vs. Tavily)
- ADR-003: Sync vs. async response model (instant vs. polling)
- ADR-004: Where to store research session state
- ADR-005: Citation verification approach

## Phase 3: How to Force AI to Review in Genuine Depth

This is the most underused skill in AI-assisted development. When you ask AI to "review this architecture", it defaults to validation mode: "this looks good, here are some minor suggestions." That is not useful.

You need to force AI into attack mode — actively trying to find failure modes, not confirm correctness.

**The five techniques that actually work:**

### Technique 1: Adversarial Prompting (Attack Mode)

```
You are conducting a security and reliability audit. Your role is NOT to validate
this design. Your role is to find failure modes.

For each component, answer:
1. What is the single most likely way this component fails in production?
2. What assumption are we making that could be wrong?
3. What happens when the dependency this component relies on goes down?
4. What happens at 10x current expected load?
5. What happens under a targeted attack?

Do not say 'this looks good.' List specific, probable failure scenarios.
```

### Technique 2: Persona-Based Review (Expert Perspectives)

Run separate review sessions, each from a specific expert perspective:

```
[Session A] You are a security architect with 15 years of distributed systems experience.
Your constraints: you assume attackers have already compromised one internal component.
Review this architecture from a threat perspective using STRIDE:
- Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege
For each STRIDE category, list specific threats against this specific design.

[Session B] You are a reliability engineer who has operated systems at 10M users.
You won't accept 'we'll handle that later.' Review this architecture for failure modes:
- What single component failure takes down the whole system?
- How do we detect failures before users do?
- What's our recovery procedure for each failure type?

[Session C] You are a developer who will implement this architecture next week.
You've never worked on a system like this before.
- What parts of this design are ambiguous or unclear to implement?
- What questions would block your work?
- Which interfaces between components aren't fully specified?
```

### Technique 3: Pre-Mortem Analysis

```
It is 6 months from now. This research tool failed in production and was taken down.
It was a significant failure: data was lost, users complained publicly, or the team
had to roll it back.

Write 5 root causes that would explain this failure.
For each root cause:
1. Why didn't we catch this during design review?
2. What assumption did we make that was wrong?
3. What specific change to the architecture would have prevented this?

Be specific — not 'the system was slow' but 'the search agents all called the same
Perplexity endpoint simultaneously, triggering rate limiting at Tier 0, causing 100%
of parallel searches to fail simultaneously with no fallback."
```

### Technique 4: Checklist-Driven Review

Forcibly evaluate against concrete, testable items — not opinions:

```
Evaluate this architecture against the following checklist.
For each item, answer: Addressed | Needs Work | Not Applicable
If 'Needs Work', describe the specific gap and how to fix it.

API CONTRACT CLARITY:
□ Every interface between components has a documented schema
□ Error codes and failure responses are specified (not 'handle errors gracefully')
□ Rate limits between internal components are defined
□ Backward compatibility plan exists for any breaking changes

FAILURE HANDLING:
□ Dependency timeout values are specified (not 'implement timeouts')
□ Cascade failure prevention is explicit (how does a search API failure not kill everything?)
□ Data consistency during failures is documented
□ Recovery procedures are explicit, not 'will handle in operations'

OBSERVABILITY:
□ Key metrics are defined: latency, error rate, cost per query
□ Tracing strategy covers full request flow end-to-end
□ Alert thresholds are set with rationale

SECURITY:
□ Authentication mechanism specified (not 'use OAuth')
□ API keys are never in code or logs
□ Data from external search APIs is treated as untrusted input

SCALABILITY:
□ Cost at 10x load is estimated
□ Caching strategy is explicit (not 'cache where needed')
□ Rate limit strategy handles Tier 0 rate limits for search APIs
```

### Technique 5: Cross-Model Review

If you have access to more than one AI model, have the second model review the first model's architecture. Models have different training data and different blind spots.

```
[In a second AI tool] Here is a system architecture that Claude designed.
Review it critically. Focus on: what Claude might have missed, what assumptions
look wrong to you, and what you would design differently and why.
[paste architecture]
```

This often surfaces issues that a single model consistently misses.

**The validation trap:** When you ask AI 'is this good?' it answers 'yes' — because you've primed it to agree. Reframe every review as an attack: 'how would this fail?' and 'what is wrong with this?' The quality of your review is determined entirely by how hard you push AI to disagree with the design.

## Phase 4: Security Review — STRIDE for AI Systems

STRIDE is a structured threat modelling framework. For AI systems, use the STRIDE-AI extension which adds agent-specific attack vectors.

**Run this prompt against each major component:**

```
Conduct a STRIDE threat model for the [component name] in this architecture.

For each category, list specific, probable threats against this component:

Spoofing — can an attacker impersonate a legitimate caller or dependency?
Tampering — can an attacker modify data in transit or at rest?
Repudiation — can actions be denied because we lack audit trails?
Information Disclosure — can secrets, user data, or internal logic leak?
Denial of Service — how can this component be made unavailable?
Elevation of Privilege — can an unprivileged caller gain admin access?

AI-specific threats:
Prompt Injection — can user-provided research questions manipulate agent behaviour?
Data Poisoning — can search results manipulate the claims verifier?
Jailbreaking — can inputs cause agents to ignore their constraints?

For each identified threat: assign risk (High / Medium / Low) and one mitigation.
```

**Critical threats for a research tool specifically:**

| Threat | Where | Risk | Mitigation |
|--------|-------|------|------------|
| Prompt injection via search results | Claims verifier reads external content | High | Treat all search result text as untrusted; isolate it from system prompts |
| API key exposure in logs | All search API calls | High | Mask keys in all log outputs; use environment variables only |
| Citation hallucination | Report generator | High | Verify every cited URL is reachable and contains the cited text |
| Rate limit cascade | Parallel search agents | Medium | Stagger requests; implement per-API exponential backoff |
| Infinite agent loops | Orchestrator | Medium | Hard max iterations (5 rounds); token budget limits |

## Phase 5: Scalability & Reliability Review

Run the scalability-focused persona review:

```
You are a scalability engineer. Review this architecture assuming it will handle
1,000 concurrent research requests per hour at peak. Current expected load is 50/hour.

For each component, answer:
1. What is the bottleneck at current load?
2. What breaks first as load increases 10x?
3. What is the cost at 1,000 req/hour? (estimate: Perplexity Pro at $0.014/req × 3 parallel searches × 1,000 req/hour = ?)
4. What caching would reduce cost without sacrificing accuracy?
5. What is the critical path — which sequential steps determine total latency?
```

**Typical findings for a research tool:**

- **Critical path bottleneck:** Sequential steps (decompose → search → verify → report) that can't be parallelised add up. Each adds 3–10 seconds. Target: decompose in parallel with first search; start report generation as soon as first verified findings return.
- **Cost at scale:** 3 parallel searches × $0.014 (Perplexity Pro) + 1 Exa search ($0.007) × 1,000 requests = ~$49/hour. Caching repeated questions saves 20–40% at scale.
- **Rate limits:** Perplexity Tier 0 = 5 RPM. At 1,000 req/hour = 16.7 req/min — already over Tier 0. Plan: upgrade to Tier 1+ or implement queue-based throttling.

**The Rubber Duck Review — expose gaps by explaining your plan:**

```
I'm going to explain this architecture to you step by step. After each step,
ask me clarifying questions that expose gaps in my plan.
Don't accept vague answers — push for specifics.

Step 1: When a user submits a question, the API gateway receives it and...
[explain your design in plain English]
```

The questions AI asks when you explain — "how do you handle partial failures?" "what defines 'enough' sources?" "what if two sub-questions return contradictory claims?" — reveal design gaps that formal review misses.

## Phase 6: Implementation Planning — From Architecture to Tasks

Once the architecture survives review, generate the implementation plan. AI-generated plans need specific structure to be useful.

**Work Breakdown Structure prompt:**

```
Generate a Work Breakdown Structure for implementing this research tool architecture:
[paste final architecture]

Format:
Level 1: Phases (Design, Development, Testing, Deployment)
Level 2: Major deliverables per phase
Level 3: Work packages
Level 4: Individual tasks

For every task:
- Task description (2–3 sentences)
- Role responsible
- Estimated duration
- Hard dependencies (which tasks must finish first)
- Deliverable output

Verify: all Level 3 work packages for a Level 2 deliverable sum to 100% of that deliverable.
```

**Example WBS output for the research tool:**

```
Phase 1: Foundation (Week 1)
├── 1.1 API Integration
│   ├── 1.1.1 Perplexity API setup + authentication (1d)
│   ├── 1.1.2 Exa AI integration + neural search test (1d)
│   ├── 1.1.3 Tavily integration + auto-parameters test (0.5d)
│   └── 1.1.4 Parallel execution with asyncio.gather (1.5d)
Phase 2: Core Agents (Weeks 2–3)
├── 2.1 Question Decomposer
│   ├── 2.1.1 Decomposition prompt engineering (2d)
│   └── 2.1.2 Output validation (sub-questions answerable by search) (1d)
├── 2.2 Claims Verifier
│   ├── 2.2.1 Source triangulation logic (2d)
│   ├── 2.2.2 Contradiction detection (1d)
│   └── 2.2.3 Confidence scoring (1d)
Phase 3: Pipeline Integration (Week 4)
Phase 4: Testing & Hardening (Week 5)
```

**Dependency mapping:**

```
For each task in this WBS, identify:
- Hard dependencies (must complete before this task starts)
- Soft dependencies (helpful to complete first, but can overlap)
- External blockers (API keys, vendor approvals, third-party access)

Output a dependency graph and highlight the critical path —
the longest chain of dependent tasks that determines minimum project duration.
```

**Risk-adjusted scheduling:**

```
For each task rated medium or high complexity, add a risk buffer.
Formula: risk buffer = (probability of delay) × (estimated delay if it occurs)

Example:
Task: Multi-agent orchestration implementation
Base estimate: 10 days
Risk: Prompt engineering for reliable decomposition is uncertain — 60% chance of 5-day delay
Buffer: 0.6 × 5 = 3 days
Adjusted estimate: 13 days

Apply this to all tasks and output the revised, risk-adjusted project schedule.
```

## Phase 7: Reviewing the Implementation Plan

The implementation plan itself needs review before work starts. Use the same adversarial approach:

**Pre-mortem on the plan:**

```
Assume this implementation plan failed — the project delivered 3 months late
and had critical bugs in production.

Write 5 root causes of the failure that trace back to flaws in this plan:
[paste WBS and schedule]

For each:
1. Which task or dependency assumption was wrong?
2. What did the plan fail to account for?
3. What change to the plan would have prevented this?
```

**Definition of Done — force testable acceptance criteria:**

```
For each major feature in this plan, write testable acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format.

Feature: Question decomposer
Given: A complex research question (e.g., 'What are the implications of AI on healthcare costs?')
When: Passed to the decomposer agent
Then: Returns 3–5 specific sub-questions, each answerable by a single web search
And: No sub-question is a restatement of the original question
And: Together the sub-questions cover the full scope of the original question

Write criteria for: parallel search, claims verifier, contradiction detection, report generator, rate limit handling.
```

**The interface-first verification check:**

```
Before any implementation starts, verify every interface between components is fully defined.

For each interface in the architecture, confirm:
- Request format (schema, required fields, types)
- Response format (success schema, error schema)
- Error codes and what each means
- Rate limits or quotas
- What happens when the downstream component is unavailable

List any interface that is underspecified. These are blockers — work cannot start
on either side of the interface until both are specified.
```

## Phase 8: Building It — AI as Your Implementation Partner

With a reviewed architecture and verified implementation plan, you're ready to build. Use AI differently at each stage.

**Starting a component: interface-first prompt**

```
I'm implementing the Question Decomposer component. Here is its specification:
- Input: research_question (string)
- Output: list of 3–5 sub_questions (list of strings)
- Constraint: each sub-question must be answerable by a single web search
- Constraint: together they must cover the full scope of the original question

Generate:
1. The function signature with type hints
2. The prompt template that produces reliable decomposition
3. A validation function that checks the output meets constraints
4. Three test cases with expected outputs
```

**The core parallel search pattern:**

```python
import asyncio
import httpx

async def search_perplexity(query: str, client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> dict:
    response = await client.post(
        "https://api.perplexity.ai/chat/completions",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {PERPLEXITY_KEY}"},
        json={
            "model": "sonar-pro",
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": query}],
            "web_search_options": {"search_context_size": "high"}
        }
    )
    return response.json()

async def search_exa(query: str, client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> dict:
    response = await client.post(
        "https://api.exa.ai/search",
        headers={"x-api-key": EXA_KEY},
        json={"query": query, "num_results": 5, "contents": {"highlights": True}}
    )
    return response.json()

async def parallel_search(sub_questions: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30.0) as client:
        tasks = [
            search_perplexity(q, client) for q in sub_questions
        ] + [
            search_exa(q, client) for q in sub_questions[:2]  # Exa on first 2 for cost control
        ]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)
    # Filter out exceptions (rate limits, timeouts) — degrade gracefully
    return [r for r in results if not isinstance(r, Exception)]
```

**Rate limit handling — exponential backoff:**

```python
async def search_with_backoff(search_fn, query: str, max_retries: int = 3):
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            return await search_fn(query)
        except httpx.HTTPStatusError as e:
            if e.response.status_code == 429:  # Rate limited
                wait = 2 ** attempt  # 1s, 2s, 4s
                await asyncio.sleep(wait)
            else:
                raise
    raise RuntimeError(f"Max retries exceeded for query: {query}")
```

**Claims triangulation prompt:**

```
You are a fact-checker. You have received findings from multiple search sources.
Your job is to identify which claims are supported, disputed, or unverified.

For each claim in these findings:
1. How many sources support it? (count)
2. Does any source contradict it? (yes/no + which)
3. Assign confidence: HIGH (3+ sources agree), MEDIUM (2 agree, none contradict), LOW (1 source only)
4. Flag as DISPUTED if any sources directly contradict each other

Findings:
[paste merged search results]

Output: A structured list of claims with confidence ratings and source citations.
```

**Citation verification — never trust, always verify:**

```python
import httpx

async def verify_citation(url: str, claimed_excerpt: str) -> bool:
    """Fetch URL and check the claimed excerpt actually exists on the page."""
    try:
        response = await httpx.AsyncClient().get(
            f"https://r.jina.ai/{url}",  # Jina Reader converts to clean markdown
            headers={"Accept": "application/json"},
            timeout=10.0
        )
        page_content = response.json().get("data", {}).get("content", "")
        # Check if key phrases from excerpt appear on the actual page
        key_phrases = claimed_excerpt.split()[:5]  # First 5 words
        return all(phrase.lower() in page_content.lower() for phrase in key_phrases)
    except Exception:
        return False  # Can't verify = don't cite
```

**Iterative implementation review — run after each component:**

```
I've implemented the [component]. Here is the code:
[paste code]

Review against these criteria:
1. Does it match the interface specification we defined?
2. Does it handle the failure modes identified in the architecture review?
3. Are there any prompt injection vulnerabilities? (check if external data touches system prompts)
4. Does it respect the API rate limits we planned for?
5. Is the error handling specific or does it swallow exceptions silently?

Don't just validate — find what's wrong.
```

**The 'no vague answers' rule:** When AI generates implementation code, push back on anything vague. 'Handle errors gracefully' is not a plan — ask 'specifically what happens when Perplexity returns a 429? What happens when Exa times out? What happens when all three APIs fail simultaneously?' The specificity of your questions determines the robustness of what gets built.

## Phase 9: AI Code Review — Before You Call It Done

Once a component is written, always run it through AI review before marking it complete. Not a single validation pass — a structured multi-angle review that specifically looks for what's wrong.

**The structured code review prompt:**

```
Review this code. Do NOT tell me what it does — I know what it does.
Your job is to find problems. Go through each category:

1. CORRECTNESS: Does the logic match the specification?
   Spec: [paste the interface spec you defined earlier]
   — Does it handle all inputs the spec allows?
   — Does it produce exactly the output the spec requires?
   — Are there edge cases the spec covers that this code ignores?

2. FAILURE HANDLING: What happens when things go wrong?
   — Which exceptions are swallowed silently (bare except or pass)?
   — Which failures leave the system in a corrupt or unknown state?
   — Is there any code path that fails without logging why?

3. SECURITY: Is this code safe when given malicious input?
   — Can any external data (search results, API responses) reach a system prompt or eval()?
   — Are API keys or secrets ever logged or included in error messages?
   — Is user input validated before it's used in a query or URL?

4. RELIABILITY: Will this hold up under real conditions?
   — Are timeouts set on all external calls? What are the values?
   — Does it respect the rate limits of every API it calls?
   — What happens if an API is slow (30+ seconds) rather than failing fast?

5. DEPENDENCIES: Are all imports and dependencies correct?
   — List every import. Are all of them actually used?
   — Are there any imports that might not be installed by default?
   — Does any import assume a specific version of a library?

For each issue: rate it Critical / Major / Minor and give the specific fix.
```

**Security-focused deep review — run this separately:**

```
Focus only on security. Review this code for:

1. Injection risks: Can any string from an external API response end up inside
   a prompt, SQL query, shell command, or URL without sanitisation?

2. Secret exposure: Are API keys, tokens, or credentials:
   - Hardcoded anywhere in the source?
   - Included in log statements?
   - Returned in error messages that could reach a client?
   - Stored in variables named with obvious patterns that suggest plain text?

3. Trust boundaries: Is there any point where the code treats data from
   an external source (search APIs, user input) as trusted?
   External data is untrusted. Show me every place it's used and whether
   it's properly isolated.

4. Dependency risk: Does this code rely on any package that:
   - Is not maintained (last commit > 1 year ago)?
   - Has known CVEs in the version range used?
   - Is fetched at runtime rather than pinned?

List every issue you find, even if it seems unlikely to be exploited.
```

**Reviewing AI-generated code specifically:**

AI-generated code has characteristic failure modes. Run this prompt after any AI-generated implementation:

```
This code was generated by an AI. Review it specifically for AI generation patterns
that cause production problems:

1. Plausible but wrong: Does any function call use an API method or parameter
   that sounds right but may not exist? (AI hallucinates library APIs.)
   List every external library call and confirm the method signature is real.

2. Happy-path only: Does the code only handle the success case?
   Trace what happens when: the API returns an empty result, the API returns
   a 500 error, the response schema is different from expected, a required
   field is missing from the response.

3. Stub code: Is there any function body that's just 'pass', 'TODO',
   'return None', or a placeholder that needs real implementation?

4. Inconsistent error handling: Are some functions raising exceptions while
   others silently return None or empty results? Pick one pattern and apply it everywhere.

5. Unused code: Are there imports, variables, or functions that are defined
   but never called? These suggest the AI wrote scaffolding it didn't finish.
```

## Phase 10: Build Verification — Does It Actually Run?

Code that passes review still needs to be verified as runnable. AI can help you catch build and startup errors before you invest time in debugging them at runtime.

**Step 1 — Generate the dependency file:**

```
Here is my complete source code:
[paste all files]

Generate:
1. A requirements.txt (or package.json / pyproject.toml) listing every dependency
   with a pinned version that is currently stable and maintained
2. A .env.example file listing every environment variable the code needs,
   with a description of what each is and where to get it
3. Any system-level dependencies (e.g., Playwright browser binaries for Firecrawl)

For each dependency, check: is this the most recent stable version? Does it have
known breaking changes in the version after the one you're pinning?
```

**Step 2 — Have AI trace the startup path for errors:**

```
Trace through what happens when this application starts for the first time
on a clean machine. Walk through every step:

1. Environment variables: which are loaded first? What happens if one is missing
   or malformed? Does the app crash immediately or fail silently later?
2. Import chain: in what order do modules import? Is there a circular import?
   Does any module execute code at import time (not in a function)?
3. Initialisation: are any clients or connections set up at startup?
   What happens if the external service is unavailable at startup time?
4. First request: trace the first real request end-to-end. What can fail
   between 'receive request' and 'return response'?

For each step, identify: what can go wrong, what the error would look like,
and how to make the failure obvious rather than silent.
```

**Step 3 — Generate a smoke test:**

A smoke test is a minimal script that confirms the application starts and basic functionality works, without running the full test suite.

```
Write a smoke test script for this application.

The smoke test should:
1. Import all modules (confirm no import errors)
2. Instantiate all major classes / initialise all major components
3. Run one end-to-end request with a simple, known input
4. Verify the output has the expected structure (not just 'something was returned')
5. Print a clear PASS or FAIL with the reason

The smoke test should complete in under 30 seconds and require no manual inspection.
If it passes, I should be confident the application starts and handles the happy path.
```

**Step 4 — Have AI check for common runtime errors before you run it:**

```
Before I run this code, list every runtime error that is likely to occur
on the first run, based on reading the code alone.

Common runtime errors to check for:
- Missing environment variables (KeyError on os.environ)
- Incorrect API response parsing (KeyError or IndexError when shape is wrong)
- Async functions called without await (coroutine never awaited)
- Type mismatches (passing a string where a list is expected)
- File path assumptions that don't hold on all operating systems
- Rate limit errors that aren't caught on the first real API call

For each likely error: where in the code, what triggers it, how to fix it before running.
```

**Step 5 — The iterative fix-and-reverify loop:**

When you do hit errors (you will), use AI to diagnose and fix them without guessing:

```
I ran the application and got this error:
[paste full stack trace, not just the last line]

Here is the relevant code:
[paste the function or module that caused the error]

Do not just fix the symptom. Tell me:
1. What is the root cause (not just which line failed)?
2. What assumption in the code is wrong?
3. What is the correct fix?
4. Are there any other places in the codebase with the same assumption that
   would cause the same error?
```

**The full stack trace rule:** Always paste the full error output — not just the final error line. The root cause is almost always in the middle of the trace, not at the end. Pasting only the last line is the single most common reason AI gives a wrong diagnosis.

**Build verification checklist:**

| Check | How to verify | Common failure |
|-------|--------------|----------------|
| Dependencies install | `pip install -r requirements.txt` with no errors | Pinned version incompatible with Python version |
| Imports resolve | `python -c "import your_module"` | Missing package or circular import |
| Env vars present | Startup check prints loaded config | Variable name typo in .env |
| Smoke test passes | Run smoke test script | API key invalid or network blocked |
| First real request | Submit a test query end-to-end | Rate limit hit immediately |
| Error path works | Simulate API failure (wrong key) | Exception not caught, app crashes |

sections.title: Run the Full Lifecycle on Your Own Research Tool
sections.content:
This workshop runs the complete 10-phase lifecycle. Work through it with a real tool idea — this course's research assistant, or any AI-powered tool you actually want to build. Each phase builds on the previous; save your outputs.

**Phase 1 — Requirements (20 minutes)**

Start a Claude conversation and run the requirements extraction sequence:
1. Describe your tool in 3–5 sentences. Ask Claude to ask clarifying questions.
2. Extract functional requirements (FR-01, FR-02...) with Must Have / Should Have ratings.
3. Run the non-functional requirements prompt. Are there NFRs you hadn't considered?

Deliver: a structured requirements document with 10+ FRs and 5+ NFRs.

**Phase 2 — Architecture (20 minutes)**

1. Run the System Context prompt. Generate the C4Context Mermaid diagram.
2. Run the Container Architecture prompt. Generate the L2 diagram.
3. Generate 3 ADRs for your most important decisions.

Deliver: two C4 diagrams (paste into a Mermaid renderer to visualise) and 3 ADRs.

**Phase 3 — Deep Review (30 minutes)**

Run at least three of the five review techniques against your architecture:
1. Adversarial review (attack mode prompt)
2. Security architect persona (STRIDE categories)
3. Pre-mortem (assume failure, find root causes)
4. Checklist-driven review (mark each item Addressed/Needs Work/N-A)
5. Rubber duck explanation (explain your design, have AI ask clarifying questions)

For each review: list the issues found and the specific changes needed.

**Phase 4 — Implementation Plan (20 minutes)**

1. Generate the WBS for your tool.
2. Run dependency mapping — identify the critical path.
3. Apply risk buffers to high-complexity tasks.
4. Run the pre-mortem on the plan itself.

Deliver: a risk-adjusted project schedule with clear task ownership.

**Phase 5 — Build One Component (30 minutes)**

Choose the component you understand best and implement it:
1. Write the interface specification first (inputs, outputs, errors).
2. Run the interface-first implementation prompt.
3. Generate test cases with expected outputs.

Deliver: a first-pass implementation ready for review.

**Phase 6 — AI Code Review (20 minutes)**

Now run the component through the three-layer code review:
1. Run the structured code review prompt (correctness, failure handling, security, reliability, dependencies).
2. Run the AI-generated code patterns review (plausible-but-wrong, happy-path only, stub code, inconsistent errors, unused code).
3. Fix every Critical issue. Fix every Major issue or document why you're accepting the risk.

Deliver: a reviewed component with a documented list of issues found and how each was resolved.

**Phase 7 — Build Verification (20 minutes)**

1. Run the dependency generation prompt — get requirements.txt and .env.example.
2. Run the startup path trace — have AI identify what fails on a clean machine.
3. Generate the smoke test script.
4. Run the startup path check for likely runtime errors.
5. If you can actually run the code: run the smoke test and fix any failures using the full-stack-trace diagnosis prompt.

Deliver: a running smoke test with a PASS result, or a documented list of remaining issues.

**Reflection (10 minutes):**
1. Which review technique found the most significant issue in the architecture?
2. What did the code review surface that you hadn't noticed while writing?
3. What would have broken on the first run if you hadn't done build verification?
4. Which phase would you have skipped if doing this solo — and what would have gone wrong?
5. What would you do differently next time?

sections.question: You've generated an architecture with AI and run one validation pass asking 'does this look good?' AI responds with a few minor suggestions and says the design is solid. What should you do?
options: Proceed to implementation — AI validated the design
Run at least 3 adversarial reviews using different techniques (adversarial prompting, persona-based review, pre-mortem), since validation-mode review almost never surfaces real failure modes
Ask a second AI model the same question and average their feedback
Add more components to the architecture until AI finds something to criticise
sections.explanation: An AI asked 'does this look good?' will almost always say yes — you've primed it to validate. One validation pass finds surface issues at best. The techniques that find real problems are: adversarial prompting ('how would this fail?'), persona-based review ('as a security architect, what are the STRIDE threats?'), and pre-mortem ('assume this failed — why?'). Run at least 3 of these before trusting the architecture. A second model's review (C) can help but isn't a substitute for adversarial framing. Adding components (D) doesn't address the review quality problem.

sections.title: Workshop A — Tool Architecture and Planning
sections.content:
Plan your AI research tool before writing any code.

**Step 1 — Define the exact problem** your research tool solves. Spend 10 minutes on this — the clearer the problem, the simpler the tool.

**Step 2 — Ask Claude** to help you choose the right architecture:
```
Help me choose the right architecture for this AI research tool:
[describe your tool]

Compare these approaches:
1. Simple LLM wrapper (just call Claude with a system prompt)
2. RAG over a document corpus
3. Agentic loop with web search tools
4. Hybrid (which combination?)

For my use case, which approach delivers the most value with the least complexity?
```

**Step 3 — Choose the simplest architecture** that meets your requirements.

**Step 4 — Write a one-page technical spec** before starting development.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build, Test, and Iterate
sections.content:
Execute the full development lifecycle for your research tool.

**Step 1 — Build the MVP** using Claude Code.

**Step 2 — Define your test corpus:** 20 research questions the tool should be able to answer.

**Step 3 — Run all 20 questions.** Score each answer: Correct (2), Partially correct (1), Wrong (0).

**Step 4 — Analyse failures:** For wrong answers, is the problem retrieval (right information wasn't found), generation (right information was found but answer was wrong), or scope (question was outside the tool's design)?

**Step 5 — Fix the top failure mode** and re-test the affected questions.

sections.title: Workshop C — Performance and Cost Optimization
sections.content:
Optimise your research tool for production use.

**Step 1 — Measure baseline performance:**
- Average response time (seconds)
- Average cost per query (tokens × price)
- P95 response time (95th percentile)

**Step 2 — Profile where time and cost are spent:** Is most time in retrieval, embedding, or generation?

**Step 3 — Apply the top optimisations based on the profile:**
- Expensive generation → switch to a cheaper model or shorter prompts
- Slow retrieval → optimise FAISS configuration or add a cache
- Slow embedding → use a local embedding model instead of API calls

**Step 4 — Re-measure after each optimisation.** Did it improve the bottleneck without degrading quality?

sections.title: Workshop D — Documentation and Handoff
sections.content:
Document your research tool for long-term maintainability.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code** to generate documentation:
```
Create documentation for this research tool:
1. README.md: what it does, how to install, how to use (with examples)
2. ARCHITECTURE.md: how it works technically, component diagram, data flow
3. OPERATIONS.md: how to update the knowledge base, troubleshoot common issues, monitor performance
4. DEVELOPMENT.md: how to run tests, add new features, contribute changes
```

**Step 2 — Review each document** for accuracy — AI-generated docs often need factual corrections.

**Step 3 — Publish the tool** (GitHub, or internal deployment).

**Step 4 — Onboard one user:** Have a colleague use the tool and document their questions. These questions become FAQ additions to the docs.

sections.question: You build a research tool that consistently returns high-quality answers during testing but produces poor answers in production. What is the most likely cause?
options: Production servers are slower and reduce AI quality
Distribution shift: production queries differ from your test corpus — real users ask different types of questions, use different vocabulary, or explore edge cases you didn't anticipate
You need to increase the server capacity
sections.explanation: Test data rarely represents production query distribution perfectly. Your test corpus was designed by you, reflecting how you think about the problem. Real users bring unexpected question formulations, unusual topics, adversarial inputs, and use cases you didn't anticipate. Fix: (1) collect production queries and add them to your test corpus; (2) monitor production answer quality metrics; (3) regularly review a sample of production queries for quality; (4) add a user feedback mechanism.

sections.question: A colleague says "just use Perplexity" instead of building a custom research tool. When is building your own tool genuinely worth it?
options: Always — custom tools are always better
When Perplexity cannot do what you need: private data (Perplexity accesses only public web), domain-specific retrieval quality, integration with internal systems, or cost efficiency at high volume
When you want to learn how to build it
sections.explanation: Build vs buy has a clear framework: build when existing tools fundamentally cannot meet your requirements. Perplexity is excellent for public web research. Building your own tool adds value when: the data is private (internal documents, proprietary databases), you need integration with internal systems, the domain requires specialised retrieval (medical literature, legal documents, code), or you're running at a volume where per-query costs make a custom system cheaper. If Perplexity meets your needs, use it — your engineering time is valuable.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 18-7 — and the Advanced AI Mastery track.** You now have a complete methodology for building AI-powered tools professionally: requirements extraction, AI-assisted architecture design, exhaustive multi-technique review, risk-adjusted implementation planning, and iterative AI-partnered implementation. The gap between people who build working AI systems and those who get stuck is almost never knowledge of AI capabilities — it's process. Now you have the process.
